title: Metropolitan Police live facial recognition flags David Cheneler, a sex offender in breach of his court order, alone with a six-year-old girl and carrying a lock knife at Denmark Hill
summary: The Metropolitan Police's Live Facial Recognition cameras identified David Cheneler, a sex offender, alone with a six-year-old girl on 10 January 2025, and he was jailed for two years.
account: In January 2025 Metropolitan Police Live Facial Recognition cameras on a van at Denmark Hill identified David Cheneler, 73. BBC News reports that officers stopped him on 10 January 2025. He was under a 2019 Sexual Offences Prevention Order that barred him from being alone with children under 14. The order followed a 2010 conviction for 15 counts of indecent assault on a female under 16 and five of gross indecency with a child. Officers found him with a six-year-old girl that he had collected from school for her mother. The mother did not know his history. A lock knife was hidden in his belt buckle. He pleaded guilty at Wimbledon Magistrates' Court on 13 January 2025 to breaching the order and possessing an offensive weapon. On 20 May 2025 Kingston Crown Court jailed him for two years. On 4 July 2025 the Met announced more than 1,000 arrests through live facial recognition and published Cheneler's case as one of its examples. On 21 April 2026 the High Court dismissed a challenge to the Met's policy on live facial recognition. It held that the policy is lawful, including its watchlists of offenders under court orders. The judges said that they had not been asked to consider whether the technology is effective. The claimants were Silkie Carlo of Big Brother Watch and Shaun Thompson, who had been misidentified by the system at London Bridge. In May 2026 William Page of Birmingham Law School wrote that Thompson intends to appeal.
purpose: The Met deploys Live Facial Recognition cameras on police vans to identify people of interest and alert officers. Its LFR lead, Lindsey Chiswick, describes the aim as using data and technology to identify offenders that pose a risk to our communities. Identifying a sex offender in breach of his order was that purpose.
system: Live Facial Recognition (LFR) cameras mounted on a Metropolitan Police van
segment: Law enforcement use of live facial recognition in public places

ratings.reason: A six-year-old girl was taken out of unsupervised contact with a man convicted of 15 counts of indecent assault on a female under 16. He had collected her from school twice before and was carrying a lock knife. The Met's officer said only that abuse was possible, and no allegation about this occasion is reported.

A registered sex offender in breach of his order was jailed for two years. The Met presents this as removing a dangerous offender from the streets. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor tags the same event with harm types for human rights, psychological harm, reputation and the public interest. On 21 April 2026 the High Court held that the Met's policy is lawful, and the judges said that they had not considered whether the technology is effective. The wider benefit is therefore contested.

ai_role.statement: The LFR system did the identification. Cameras on the back of a van at Denmark Hill matched Cheneler's face and alerted officers, Southwark News reports. Finding the child and the knife, the arrest, the charges and the sentence were human and judicial acts. The offense itself existed only because of his 2019 order. The counterfactual is the Met's own hedge. DC Adam Pearce said it is possible that, had he not been identified, Cheneler could have gone on to abuse the child. No allegation about this occasion is reported. The readable source does not name the vendor or algorithm. The Met's press release is not among the sources.

produced_by: A van-mounted LFR deployment at Denmark Hill in January 2025 and a face the system was able to identify. The match alerted officers on the spot.
Officers who stopped him at once and found the child and the lock knife hidden in his belt buckle. They knew the terms of his 2019 Sexual Offences Prevention Order.
A court record of the order and his 2010 convictions. This turned the stop into a guilty plea for breaching the order and possessing an offensive weapon.
must_hold: The person must be known to the system and subject to conditions that make his presence with a child an offense. The benefit depends on the prior order, not on the camera alone.
Officers must verify the match and intervene immediately. The child was found only because he was stopped on the spot.

The deployment must be lawful and proportionate. The OECD Monitor files this same event under human-rights, psychological, reputational and public-interest harm types. The protective benefit therefore sits beside a contested surveillance practice.

display.answer: Southwark News quotes the investigating officer, Adam Pearce, and reports the court outcomes. Biometric Update reports the Met's announcement of 4 July 2025, which used Cheneler's case as an example. The High Court judgment of 21 April 2026 concerns the lawfulness of the Met's policy on live facial recognition.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: The Metropolitan Police's Live Facial Recognition cameras identified David Cheneler, a sex offender, alone with a six-year-old girl on 10 January 2025, and he was jailed for two years.
fields.account: In January 2025 Metropolitan Police Live Facial Recognition cameras on a van at Denmark Hill identified David Cheneler, 73. BBC News reports that officers stopped him on 10 January 2025. He was under a 2019 Sexual Offences Prevention Order that barred him from being alone with children under 14. The order followed a 2010 conviction for 15 counts of indecent assault on a female under 16 and five of gross indecency with a child. Officers found him with a six-year-old girl that he had collected from school for her mother. The mother did not know his history. A lock knife was hidden in his belt buckle. He pleaded guilty at Wimbledon Magistrates' Court on 13 January 2025 to breaching the order and possessing an offensive weapon. On 20 May 2025 Kingston Crown Court jailed him for two years. On 4 July 2025 the Met announced more than 1,000 arrests through live facial recognition and published Cheneler's case as one of its examples. On 21 April 2026 the High Court dismissed a challenge to the Met's policy on live facial recognition. It held that the policy is lawful, including its watchlists of offenders under court orders. The judges said that they had not been asked to consider whether the technology is effective. The claimants were Silkie Carlo of Big Brother Watch and Shaun Thompson, who had been misidentified by the system at London Bridge. In May 2026 William Page of Birmingham Law School wrote that Thompson intends to appeal.

produced_by: A van-mounted LFR deployment at Denmark Hill in January 2025 and a face the system was able to identify. The match alerted officers on the spot.
Officers who stopped him at once and found the child and the lock knife hidden in his belt buckle. They knew the terms of his 2019 Sexual Offences Prevention Order.
A court record of the order and his 2010 convictions. This turned the stop into a guilty plea for breaching the order and possessing an offensive weapon.
must_hold: The person must be known to the system and subject to conditions that make his presence with a child an offense. The benefit depends on the prior order, not on the camera alone.
Officers must verify the match and intervene immediately. The child was found only because he was stopped on the spot.

The deployment must be lawful and proportionate. The OECD Monitor files this same event under human-rights, psychological, reputational and public-interest harm types. The protective benefit therefore sits beside a contested surveillance practice.
